 Log in Ken Sanders, original Brewer and 1971 AL Fireman of Year, dies at 85
 November 16th, 2026 Adam McCalvy
 Share share-square--:R1qlq: MILWAUKEE -- Former right-handed reliever  Ken Sanders , one of the original Milwaukee Brewers and the 1971 American League Fireman of the Year Award winner, died over the weekend after a cancer battle, his family confirmed to the Brewers’ flagship radio station. He was 85. 
 Known as “Bulldog,” Sanders was born in St. Louis and pitched in the big leagues for the Athletics and Red Sox before being traded to the Seattle Pilots in January 1970, less than four months before that franchise moved to Milwaukee and became the Brewers. 
 Sanders wound up making the Milwaukee area his permanent home and remained proud of his contributions in the early years of the Brewers, most notably in 1971, when he posted a 1.91 ERA in 136 1/3 innings and led the Majors with 31 saves for a team that won 69 games all season. Sanders pitched in 83 games that season, tied with Alex Claudio for the Brewers' franchise record. Sanders finished 77 games, a Major League record at the time that has been eclipsed only three times since.
 Sanders followed with 17 saves and a 3.12 ERA in 62 games in 1972 before the Brewers packaged him with Ken Brett, Jim Lonborg and Earl Stephenson in a blockbuster trade to the Phillies for Bill Champion, Don Money and John Vukovich. Money went on to play 11 seasons for the Brewers and was a four-time All-Star. 
 Sanders never pitched for the Phillies. He was traded to the Twins a month later and played for Minnesota, Cleveland, the Angels, Mets and Royals through the remainder of his Major League career, which ended in 1976. After settling in Hales Corners, Wisc., Sanders was a frequent visitor to County Stadium, Miller Park and American Family Field, and he regularly represented the Brewers at public events. 
 Sanders is survived by his wife, Mary Ann, and their three adopted children: son Steven and daughters Laura and Leanne.
